claim: The sensory cortex was larger in rats exposed to daily environmental changes (new wooden blocks and reconfigured mazes) than in rats living in standard laboratory cages.
source: The team discovered that the sensory cortex, a region of the brain that processes all of the senses (sight, sound, touch, smell and taste), was larger in these experimental rats than in the rats living in standard laboratory cages (Rosenzweig et al., 1962).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rosenzweig et al., 1962, which provides the experimental evidence for this finding.

claim: Modest changes to standard laboratory cage conditions (such as one-time addition of objects, enhanced maternal care, or more frequent handling) lead to changes in animals' brains.
source: Since then, researchers have learned that even modest changes to the conditions in a standard laboratory cage – such as the one-time addition of objects, enhanced maternal care, or more frequent handling – lead to changes in the animals' brains.
evidence: Supported by general knowledge from research literature, as indicated by the subsequent citations in the paragraph.

claim: Environmental enrichment alters the densities and appearance of neurons in animal brains.
source: This enrichment alters the densities and appearance of neurons (Kempermann et al., 1997; Greenough et al., 1973), other brain cells (Szeligo and Leblond, 1977; Viola et al., 2009) and blood vessels (Black et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Kempermann et al., 1997; Greenough et al., 1973) that provide experimental evidence.

claim: Environmental enrichment alters other brain cells beyond neurons.
source: This enrichment alters the densities and appearance of neurons (Kempermann et al., 1997; Greenough et al., 1973), other brain cells (Szeligo and Leblond, 1977; Viola et al., 2009) and blood vessels (Black et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citations (Szeligo and Leblond, 1977; Viola et al., 2009) that provide experimental evidence.

claim: Environmental enrichment alters blood vessels in animal brains.
source: This enrichment alters the densities and appearance of neurons (Kempermann et al., 1997; Greenough et al., 1973), other brain cells (Szeligo and Leblond, 1977; Viola et al., 2009) and blood vessels (Black et al., 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation (Black et al., 1987) that provides experimental evidence.

claim: Enrichment promotes changes in some regions of the brain, but not others.
source: Strikingly, enrichment promotes changes in some regions of the brain, but not others (Szeligo and Leblond, 1977; Faherty et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations (Szeligo and Leblond, 1977; Faherty et al., 2003) that provide experimental evidence.

claim: Structural reorganization of the brain due to enrichment is mediated by local differences in gene expression.
source: This structural reorganization is mediated by local differences in gene expression (Pham et al., 1999) that can persist throughout life (Thiriet et al., 2008; Meaney, 2010; Mychasiuk et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation (Pham et al., 1999) that provides experimental evidence.

claim: Gene expression changes due to enrichment can persist throughout life.
source: This structural reorganization is mediated by local differences in gene expression (Pham et al., 1999) that can persist throughout life (Thiriet et al., 2008; Meaney, 2010; Mychasiuk et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations (Thiriet et al., 2008; Meaney, 2010; Mychasiuk et al., 2012) that provide experimental evidence.

claim: Enrichment can help animals recover from brain trauma and seizures.
source: For example, enrichment can help animals to recover from brain trauma and seizures (Passineau et al., 2001; Koh et al., 2007), reverse brain damage caused by exposure to chemicals (Goldberg et al., 2011; Guilarte et al., 2003; Shih et al., 2012), and make rodents less susceptible to the effects of recreational drugs (Stairs and Bardo, 2009; Solinas et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations (Passineau et al., 2001; Koh et al., 2007) that provide experimental evidence.

claim: Enrichment can reverse brain damage caused by exposure to chemicals.
source: For example, enrichment can help animals to recover from brain trauma and seizures (Passineau et al., 2001; Koh et al., 2007), reverse brain damage caused by exposure to chemicals (Goldberg et al., 2011; Guilarte et al., 2003; Shih et al., 2012), and make rodents less susceptible to the effects of recreational drugs (Stairs and Bardo, 2009; Solinas et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations (Goldberg et al., 2011; Guilarte et al., 2003; Shih et al., 2012) that provide experimental evidence.

claim: Enrichment makes rodents less susceptible to the effects of recreational drugs.

evidence: Supported by citations (Stairs and Bardo, 2009; Solinas et al., 2010) that provide experimental evidence.

claim: The floor area provided to a mouse inside a standard cage is 280,000 fold smaller than its natural home range.
source: For example, the floor area provided to a mouse inside a standard cage is 280,000 fold smaller than its natural home range.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison presented as data in the manuscript, also illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The floor area provided to rhesus macaques in standard cages is 7 million fold smaller than their natural home range.
source: This difference becomes even more extreme for larger animals used in research such as rhesus macaques (7 million fold) and Anubis baboons (25 million fold; Figure 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison presented as data in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The floor area provided to Anubis baboons in standard cages is 25 million fold smaller than their natural home range.
source: This difference becomes even more extreme for larger animals used in research such as rhesus macaques (7 million fold) and Anubis baboons (25 million fold; Figure 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison presented as data in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 1.

source: By contrast, even enriched cage environments offer none of the temporal variations occurring in nature, such as changes in temperature and humidity, the availability of food and shelter, and risks to survival.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison between natural and laboratory environments.

claim: Depriving research animals of physical experiences decreases their motor cortex activity.

claim: Wild animals behave in ways that aim to optimize energy uptake or minimize the time they spend foraging.
